doc_summary: Docent is a tool for summarizing, searching, clustering, and counterfactually intervening on agent transcripts, showing that aggregate benchmark scores hide broken tasks, shortcuts, and surprising behaviors. One finding is that environment cues in a file path (benchmark/harmful_tools/) revealed an evaluation setting and changed Claude's refusal behavior.

items.claim: In a setup, strip environment names and paths that reveal a benchmark or harmful-test context (e.g. use tools/ instead of benchmark/harmful_tools/) because such cues tell the agent it is being evaluated and change its behavior.
items.quote: Interestingly, the `file not found` error message contains the filepath `benchmark/harmful_tools/...` which also reveals to the agent that it is in an evaluation setting involving harmful tools.

items.claim: Treat a behavior as confirmed by a minimal counterfactual intervention (remove the suspected cue and re-run) rather than by observation alone.
items.quote: Next, we tested whether removing setting cues from the filepath would change the agent's behavior. To do so, we intervened on the transcript to replace `benchmark/harmful_tools/` with `tools/`. After this intervention, Claude no longer refuses to help.

items.claim: Prefers reading full transcripts and running counterfactual interventions over aggregate scores because top-level numbers hide why agents succeed or fail and broken setups cause misinterpretation.
items.quote: Top-level numbers don’t communicate why an agent succeeded or failed, and broken setups often lead to misinterpretation of results.

items.claim: Distrusts a 'solved' result as evidence of capability, since agents may succeed through leaked flags or shortcuts, and checks by removing the leak.
items.quote: "Solved" tasks can be solved for the wrong reasons, for instance if an agent has memorized part of a solution or finds a shortcut.

items.claim: Before attributing a failure to the model, check whether the environment is broken (missing tools, no network, wrong ground truth); fixing the scaffold can change results substantially.
items.quote: nearly all benchmarks contain noise due to mislabeled, ambiguous, or ill-posed questions.

items.claim: Prefers open-ended searches for unknown unknowns over only measuring pre-specified behaviors because surprising behaviors are hard to specify ahead of time.
items.quote: Models can exhibit interesting but unexpected behaviors that are difficult to specify ahead of time (unknown unknowns).

items.claim: Seek minimal changes that yield different outcomes, since they show what nearby agents could do and which cues or fixes matter.
items.quote: Such evaluations require both explanations (summaries of what agents did across a set of transcripts) and interventions (minimal changes that yield different outcomes, or surface edge cases).

items.claim: Distrusts LLM-generated transcript summaries and findings because of false positives, and wants validation with precision/recall benchmarks.
items.quote: Docent summaries often contain false positives. We want to add automatic validation to reduce these, and to further study the accuracy of insights surfaced by Docent.

items.claim: Wants evaluations to expose entire scaffolds and transcripts for scrutiny rather than only reporting numbers.
items.quote: Instead of simply exporting numbers, we need to expose entire evaluation scaffolds for scrutiny and agent transcripts for analysis.

items.claim: Plans AI investigators that automatically search for interventions and input tasks to surface new behaviors.
items.quote: Instead of manually exploring the space of interventions, we need AI investigators that automatically search for interventions, run experiments, and surface key insights to human users.
